title: How does stretch fabric spring back?
teaches: Stretch from knitted loops against stretch from elastic fibre; how elastane is built and who made it; how much goes into jeans and swimwear; why stretch wears out; why blends are hard to recycle

blocks.text: Leggings stretch over a bent knee and lie flat again when the wearer stands up. An old tracksuit of cotton jersey, a common knitted cloth, stretches just as easily but keeps a bulge at the knee. Modern jeans have some give that older jeans lacked, and after a few years that give can go slack.

Lesson 4 showed why woven cloth hardly stretches along its threads: the warp and weft run straight, so a pull along either one is carried by the yarn itself, which gives only a few percent. Woven cloth stretches more on the diagonal, the **bias**, where the pull can change the angle between warp and weft. Knitted cloth is different. Its yarn runs in rows of interlocking loops, and a pull changes the shape of the loops, making them longer and narrower, long before the yarn itself is stretched. A cotton jersey can stretch by a third or more with very little force.

When knitted cotton is let go, the loops have to be pulled back into shape, and cotton fibres have little elastic recovery. After a gentle stretch the jersey recovers, but after a hard one, such as a knee bent for an hour, part of the stretch stays. Wool recovers better, which is one reason knitted wool keeps its shape longer than knitted cotton.

blocks.text: Before the 1960s, the only fibre that could stretch to several times its length and spring back was rubber. Thread of rubber wrapped in cotton or silk was used in corsets, girdles and the tops of socks, but it was heavy, perished with age and sweat, and could not be dyed. In 1958 the chemist **Joseph Shivers** at the American chemical company DuPont produced a synthetic fibre that stretched like rubber but was lighter and stronger. DuPont sold it from 1962 under the trade name **Lycra**. The fibre is called **spandex**[^spandex-name] in North America and **elastane** elsewhere.

Elastane is a polyurethane made of long chains with two kinds of segments alternating along the chain. The **soft segments** are flexible and lie coiled, like loose springs. The **hard segments** cling to the hard segments of neighbouring chains, forming fixed points that hold the chains together. When the fibre is pulled, the soft segments uncoil and the fibre can stretch to five or six times its length. When it is let go, the soft segments coil up again, and because the hard segments have held the chains in place, the fibre returns to its starting length.

A small share of elastane changes how a cloth behaves. Stretch jeans usually contain 1 to 3 percent, enough to let a woven denim give a little at the knee and hip. A T-shirt or a pair of trousers with 5 percent knitted in recovers its shape after every stretch. Swimwear, leggings and cycling shorts use 15 to 30 percent, enough to hold the cloth tight against the body. The elastane is usually hidden inside the yarn, with the main fibre wrapped around it[^core-spun], so the cloth feels like cotton or nylon rather than like elastane.

Elastane is much less durable than the fibres it is mixed with. Heat breaks down its chains, so a hot tumble dryer or a hot iron weakens it quickly. Chlorine in swimming pools attacks it, which is why swimsuits lose their grip within a season of regular use, and some are now made from elastane designed to resist chlorine. Sunlight and body oils damage it more slowly. As the fibres break, the cloth loses its recovery: jeans grow loose at the knees and waistband, and the cloth may show small puckers where broken elastane has snapped back inside the yarn.

Elastane also makes clothes harder to recycle. A recycling plant that turns old cotton into new fibre, or old polyester back into new polyester, needs a single, clean fibre to work with. A few percent of elastane mixed through every yarn is very hard to separate, and it can spoil the process. Branch lesson M7, on recycled polyester, returns to this problem.

items.ask: Why does a cotton jersey stretch more easily than a woven cotton shirt?
choices: Its loops change shape before the yarn is pulled
Its cotton fibres are more elastic than woven ones
It is made from much thinner yarn
items.why: A pull on a knit changes the shape of its loops. In a weave, the straight threads take the pull directly.

items.ask: Why can an old cotton jersey keep a bulge at the knee?
choices: Cotton cannot pull its loops back into shape
Washing has shrunk the rest of the trousers
The loops have been cut through at the knee
Cotton fibres grow longer when they are warm
items.why: The loops are pulled out of shape, and nothing in plain cotton pulls them back.

items.ask: What makes elastane spring back after a stretch?
choices: Soft segments recoil while hard segments hold the chains
It is coated with a thin layer of natural rubber
Its fibres are woven into a tight satin
Its chains are tied together by sulphur bonds
items.why: The coiled soft segments uncoil under pull and recoil when let go; the hard segments act as fixed points.

items.ask: Which habit wears out stretch in everyday clothes?
choices: Drying it in a hot tumble dryer
Washing it inside out in cold water
Storing it folded in a drawer
Hanging it to dry in the shade
items.why: Heat breaks down elastane's chains. Chlorine, sunlight and body oils damage it too.

summary: **Cotton knits stretch easily but recover poorly.** A cotton jersey stretches by a third with little force, but a hard stretch leaves a baggy knee.
**Elastane springs back.** Its coiled soft segments recoil, while hard segments hold the chains in place.
**A small share of elastane is enough.** Jeans use 1 to 3 percent and swimwear 15 to 30 percent.
**Heat and chlorine wear elastane out.** Damaged elastane lets clothes grow slack.

spandex-name.title: Fibre K and spandex
spandex-name.text: DuPont originally called the fibre Fibre K during development. The generic American name "spandex" is an anagram of "expands".

core-spun.title: Core-spun yarn
core-spun.text: In a **core-spun yarn**, a continuous filament of elastane is fed through the spinning frame under tension while staple fibres such as cotton are twisted around it. When the tension is released, the elastane contracts slightly, leaving the cotton on the outside.
